book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying

chapters.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Crichton was doing philosophy rather than science: he imagined a possibility and probed its range because it could not be tested. It frames the whole book around Malcolm's question of whether we should, not whether we can, and around the gap between what we can do and what we should do with technologies like de-extinction. It connects the film to our illusion of control, insisting there are no ghosts or magic here, only nature, and that forgetting how edible we are turns us into 'bloody smears on the teeth of a T. rex'.

Michaud and Watkins blame Crichton and Malcolm for frightening us away from science, arguing that most life does not 'find a way' and that science is the shield keeping vulnerable humanity a step ahead of extinction by meteors, plagues, and predators. They take up Rousseau's anti-Enlightenment longing to return to nature and reject it, arguing that humility comes from science itself (a 13.72-billion-year-old Earth, Sagan's 'star stuff' making us the universe become conscious of itself), not from abandoning it. Hammond, not science, embodies the real arrogance: he was so certain he could not fail that he tested the park on his own grandchildren.

Littmann surveys real de-extinction efforts (George Church's passenger pigeon, plans to clone a frozen mammoth) and asks when reviving extinct species is morally permissible. He argues that Arne Naess's deep ecology, with its 'equal right to live and blossom', fails because it projects human desires onto organisms like plants that have none, and cannot say whether species or only individuals bear rights. He instead applies Mill's utilitarianism: bring species back when doing so maximizes happiness and minimizes suffering, which permits a Jurassic Park in principle but forbids dinosaur fights and trophy hunts like Roland Tembo's, and rebukes Sattler's claim that only the people we love matter.

Freeman explains why Grant dismisses the clones as 'genetically engineered theme park monsters': a frog-DNA-patched genome is not dinosaur DNA, and nobody knows how much alteration turns a T. rex into something else, so as Wu tells Hammond the park has only reconstructed the past, never re-created it. Behavior cannot vindicate the clones either, since The Lost World's raptors grow up without elders to teach raptor behavior, and the animals must survive an ecosystem of grass, bacteria, and species that did not exist in the Cretaceous. The chapter's running puzzle of how much of an organism can change before it is no longer that organism is a Ship of Theseus problem applied to paleontology.

Shea stages the Wu-Malcolm dispute through Hume's Dialogues: Jurassic Park is an 'intelligent design' so botched that, like Philo's world of needless suffering, it points to ignorant or malicious designers rather than a perfect God, undercutting Richard Owen-style design arguments. He then explains Hammond's folly with Darwinian natural selection and memetics, treating the dinosaur-theme-park as a meme that infected InGen's investors by exploiting evolved desires for profit, fame, and importance. Hammond's fatal errors were assuming evolution 'wants' humans to survive, that complexity means better adapted, and that he could outsmart selection, which the all-female raptors breeding and life 'finding a way' quickly refute.

A pub dialogue applies Aristotle's De Anima, where the soul is the first principle of living things, to cloning: since a living clone must have an emergent, unrepeatable soul, successfully cloning dinosaurs brings new life into existence, which is good, so cloning itself is ethical. It then argues that neither unguided natural selection nor a divine dragon-slayer who nonetheless allowed cloning technology gives us reason not to revive dinosaurs, against Malcolm's 'they had their shot'. But drawing on Plato's forms, it condemns Hammond for controlling rather than merely containing: the lysine contingency and enforced sterility leave the dinosaurs shadows of what they could be, denied their natural flourishing.

Billard concedes the Stoic point that we control neither our passions nor nature ('life will always find a way', Sattler's 'you never had control'), as the bucardo cloning failure shows, but argues this proves the park rushed, not that de-extinction is impossible. Dangerousness is subjective, raptor intelligence is a logistics problem rather than a metaphysical objection, and since humans have already caused the sixth mass extinction we may have a duty to bring species back. Because revived animals would be 'neo-dinosaurs' built from fragmentary DNA, de-extinction is creation rather than resurrection, less like playing God than like the transhumanist enhancement humans already practice.

Edwards argues that gene banks assume genes are the essence of a species, which he reads as a modernized Platonism: unchanging forms written in DNA, the same craving Hammond expresses in wanting to show people 'something that wasn't an illusion'. Following Hans Jonas's reading of Darwin, in which conditions rather than essence explain what an organism is, he casts Wu as the Platonist and Malcolm's 'life finds a way' as the evolutionary rebuttal in their debate over breeding control. The moral is that freezing DNA cannot save species, because what makes an animal what it is includes the vanished environment, so we should preserve habitats rather than entrust preservation to 'the hands of engineers'.

Fitzpatrick argues that the awe Ellie feels at the brachiosaurs makes experiencing real dinosaurs so valuable that restoring them may be obligatory, and reads Malcolm's distrust of land managers as sharing Leopold's land ethic, under which firebombing Isla Nublar would be barbarism on the order of Dresden. Invoking Bentham, Mill, and Singer's expansion of the moral community (echoed in the park's dart guns), he weighs Elliot's 'Faking Nature' and Katz's charge that restored nature is a fake and an arrogance against Andrew Light's defense of respectful restoration. He concludes that Jurassic Park failed not because restoration is wrong but because Hammond restored dinosaurs for amusement, and that a careful, land-ethic-respecting de-extinction could one day be justified.

Sexton reads the park as capitalist ideology in action, quoting Marx and Engels on the ruling class controlling the means of mental production: Hammond's flea circus is the illusion we agree not to see, and Nedry's sabotage shows what happens when workers are told their poverty is their own problem. He applies Veblen's leisure class to Gennaro, who judges the night-vision goggles valuable because they are expensive, and Marx's general law of capitalist accumulation to Hammond's squeezing of wages once every other cost is beyond his control. The dinosaurs themselves figure as the exploited working class, held not by ideology but by electric fences, and when the fence falls they seize the park.

Michael Muniz argues the dinosaurs of Jurassic Park are real 'in the most important ways' - not cloned in a lab, but real whenever the film runs: they terrify, they occupy our dreams (his T. rex-at-the-window opening), and they re-actualize deep time on screen. He weighs whether the franchise is genuinely horror - preying on fear for a negative response - or something stranger, a tension between fear and excitement in which extinction itself is the source of the scare.

Stoody asks whether Hammond's dinosaurs are more than bones, blood, and DNA, and answers with Nagel's bat: there is something it is like to be eaten by a velociraptor, and even a complete neuroscience of a T. rex's brain would not reveal the bloodhound-rivaling smells it experiences. He reruns Jackson's Mary as Dr. Sattler raised in a black-and-white world who learns something new upon seeing violet West Indian Lilac berries, and rebuts the physicalist two-descriptions reply using Crichton's Michael Douglas pen name. He concludes that physicalism leaves out the what-it's-like aspect of consciousness, leaving a choice between substance dualism (dinosaur souls) and property dualism.

Kempner argues that the featherless raptors confirm Baudrillard's hyperreal: our dinosaurs are 'a real without origin or reality', like blue raspberry flavor or the never-existent brontosaurus, so the more real the clones pretend to be, the more fake they seem. He reads Wu's 'there isn't any reality here' and The Lost World's fossil-album passage as Crichton's own warnings against mistaking images for reality, while Spielberg's rejection of feathers shows the franchise teaching audiences to prefer the fake. Baudrillard himself used the film's finale, cloned dinosaurs rampaging among their fossilized ancestors in the museum, as the image of our predicament between 'our fossils and our clones'.

Karavitis maps the three films onto the history of animal ethics: Jurassic Park treats dinosaurs as property on Aristotle's ground that only rational humans matter; The Lost World adds Kant's indirect duties, where the sporting rules of Tembo's hunt express duties owed to other humans rather than to the T. rex; and Jurassic Park III moves to Tom Regan, whose 'subjects-of-a-life' with inherent value fits raptors that remember, plan, and finally choose to spare the humans. The cow and goat fed live to the raptors test how far each view protects animals we treat as mere means.

King charges human exceptionality with being speciesism and asks whether dinosaurs are persons rather than humans, testing Kant's rationality criterion and Descartes' denial of animal thought against the raptor that opens the shed door and the T. rex that spins the Explorer searching for prey. He runs the dinosaurs through Mary Anne Warren's five personhood criteria, then plays his Wittgenstein trump card: animal language would be the language of a different life-form, so the raptors' calls expressing fear and summoning help count as real communication without words. He closes with Regan's rights view, arguing that the cow and goat feeding scenes, like past denials of personhood to Native Americans and women, should shame us into showing a little respect.

holes.name: Memes (units of cultural inheritance)
holes.what: A meme is an idea or practice that replicates from mind to mind, allowing cultural change to be analyzed as an evolution parallel to genetic natural selection.
holes.why: Chapter 13's central explanation of why Hammond built the park is memetic: the dinosaur-theme-park meme infected InGen's investors by exploiting evolved desires for profit and fame.

holes.name: Transhumanism
holes.what: A movement seeking technologies that overcome fundamental human limitations, including aging and the enhancement of intellectual, physical, and psychological abilities toward a 'post-human'.
holes.why: Chapter 16 frames de-extinction and 'neo-dinosaurs' as continuous with transhumanist enhancement rather than as overreaching 'playing God'.

holes.name: Hans Jonas
holes.what: Twentieth-century philosopher of biology whose The Phenomenon of Life argues that after Darwin, conditions and environment, not changeless essence, explain what an organism is.
holes.why: Chapter 17's whole argument that genes are outdated Platonic forms and that gene banks cannot save species rests on Jonas's claim that 'conditions take the place of essence'.

holes.name: Thorstein Veblen
holes.what: Economist and social critic whose Theory of the Leisure Class analyzes conspicuous consumption, buying expensive goods to signal status rather than for use.
holes.why: Chapter 19 uses Veblen to decode Gennaro, who judges the night-vision goggles valuable because they are expensive, equating worth with price.

holes.name: The Paradox of Fiction
holes.what: The puzzle that we genuinely feel emotions for characters and events we know do not exist, although we apparently only respond emotionally to what we believe is real.
holes.why: Chapter 20 is organized around this paradox to explain why movie dinosaurs frighten and thrill us although we know they are not real.

holes.name: Mary Anne Warren
holes.what: Philosopher who proposed five criteria of personhood (consciousness, reasoning, self-driven activity, communication, self-concepts) and argued that entities meeting most of them deserve respect.
holes.why: Chapter 25 runs its 'Dino Personhood Checklist' entirely through Warren's criteria to argue that velociraptors qualify as persons.

holes.name: The Reality of Fictional Entities
holes.what: Debates over the sense in which fictional characters and events exist or are real (Meinong, Walton's make-believe).
holes.why: Muniz's chapter claims screen dinosaurs are 'real' and needs the ontology-of-fiction vocabulary.
